original: For professors, publishing in elite journals is an unavoidable part of university life. The grueling process of subjecting work to the up-or-down judgment of credentialed scholarly peers has been a cornerstone of academic culture since at least the mid-20
sampled:
th century.

But a handful of highly respected scientists are now questioning the wisdom and cost of this approach — and at least one researcher is attempting to make it easier for academics to submit work to journals with relatively little scrutiny. The idea, which advocates call “open access,” would allow scientists to submit their work to any journal of their choosing, whether their university subscribes to it or not, and would allow scientists to avoid cumbersome and sometimes opaque processes that determine whether their work is worthy of review.

The proposal is still an embryonic idea — an open-access journal has yet to appear, despite many years of advocacy by scientists and academics. But it’s making waves in the scientific community as a way to open up scientific work to a broader audience and spur innovation. The idea has become especially attractive to academics who are increasingly concerned about academic freedom and the growing influence of the private sector over universities.

original: Urban, born Jacques Pantaléon in Troyes c. 1200, was elected to the papacy in 1261. He studied canon law at Paris and served as bishop of Verdun and patriarch of Jerusalem. He hoped to keep Sicily from the
sampled:
French, so Pope Adrian IV sent Urban to Sicily in 1261. The Sicilians were very angry, and in 1264 Urban took the title "Defender of the Faith," but he was unwilling to make use of the papal arms. He expelled the French from the island and put all of the French nobles to death. He moved the capital from Palermo to Messina, where he died in 1275.

Urban was a good canonist and a strict disciplinarian, but his actions were a source of great irritation to both sides of the Papal Schism. He refused to recognize the pope as head of the Church and refused to recognize the right of the pope to excommunicate. He is known for ordering the execution of the French king John II of Naples in 1261. He is sometimes known as the "Defender of the Faith" because he was unwilling to use the papal arms. He is also called Urban of Messina because he moved the capital of the Papal States to Messina in 1275. He is also sometimes known as "Urban of the Holy Sepulcher" for his actions in Jerusalem.

sampled:
breaking heat and the lack of a cyclone season combined with low water levels in the Coral Sea, which has devastated the reef, are to blame for this summer's bleaching.
"We're seeing some corals which should have been bleached, which have lost their zooxanthellae, their photosynthetic pigments," Professor Terry Hughes, of James Cook University's Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority, told The World's host Marco Werman. "That means they no longer have a source of energy. The result is we've seen coral mortality rates of 50% already in certain areas."
"Corals are not built to withstand bleaching events like this," added Dr. James Cook scientist Tony Blakely. "It's a death sentence for most of the corals in those areas."
Hughes said there was no doubt that the current event was the worst on record for the reef. "If we get no cyclone event, which hasn't happened before, we can't see the top half of the reef, which means bleaching has occurred everywhere. Neutrophils are a type of white blood cell that helps heal damaged tissues and resolve infections. Neutrophil blood levels increase naturally in response to infections, injuries, and other types
sampled:
of tissue damage. Neutrophils play a central role in the body’s natural immune response to disease.
The neutrophils release a number of signaling factors that activate different types of immune cells in the bloodstream. These include:
TNF-alpha Neutrophil cytokines (including granulocyte colony stimulating factor, interferon gamma and interleukin-6) Interleukin-2, interleukin-4, interleukin-6, interleukin-7, interleukin-8 and granulocyte macrophage-colony stimulating factor, or GM-CSF Neutrophil enzymes L-cysteine and quinine

sampled:
wander the ground floor, where their artworks are displayed.

The latest chapter in an often fraught struggle between artist-decorators and the state came to a head in April, when an administrative tribunal ruled that a city law that allowed the council to order a renovation of the building was flawed.

The building, which houses one of the largest and most diverse collections of contemporary art in Europe, is also the site of two highly successful “aftersquats”, where visitors can freely wander through rooms displaying the work of dozens of artists, including Yves Klein.

The collection itself dates back to 1968 and the work of the late artist-decorator Marcel Duchamp. It was bequeathed to the French state in 1981 and has been cared for by a government institution ever since.

The latest dispute came about as a result of a renovation that began in 2012 and was partially paid for by a government fund, which allocated 1.5 million euros ($1.7 million) for the work.

City hall plans to replace the old floor and walls, but keep the original layout, which the artists say is crucial to preserving their hard-earned legacy.

pland, water demand and water supply, habitat changes and the role of forestry, and the role of biodiversity.

As usual, Professor Jack Ponton (Letters, 8 July) cuts through all the smoke and mirrors erected by the renewables industries to give the facts.
He points out the absurdity of the regular and monotonous claims from the wind industry that
sampled:
they are low carbon sources of power, when, in actual fact, they are a tiny and unpredictable and almost completely intermittent source of power, which in Britain contribute virtually nothing.

As for wind, it is a highly subsidised energy technology which can only be expected to provide a tiny contribution to the UK’s increasing power requirements. The vast majority of our energy comes from the conventional sources of fossil fuels. The problem of the current electricity shortage is primarily down to the lack of supply of gas from the North Sea, which has led to the use of expensive imported gas, which raises the costs of power, and the lack of supply of power from the traditional base load power stations. Unfortunately, these large power stations cannot easily be modified to provide a much needed supply of power at times of peak demand. The problem has been exacerbated by the use of the ageing coal fired stations in the east of England, which have to be run in order to provide a small supply of power to meet the peak demand. The closure of these coal fired stations in favour of the renewable energy sources is a mistake. If the coal and gas supply chains cannot be improved to meet the current demand, then we need to focus on building new nuclear power stations.
